claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater plastic strain than commercially pure tungsten under identical high-temperature mechanical loading.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater toughness and resistance to crack initiation and propagation than commercially pure tungsten under identical high-temperature mechanical loading.
Mixing W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces severe local atomic lattice distortions in the alloy.
The lattice distortions generate localized misfit stresses.
The localized misfit stresses modify dislocation mobility.
Modified dislocation mobility enhances dislocation activity in WTaTiVZr.
Enhanced dislocation activity promotes work hardening in WTaTiVZr.
The proposed dislocation and work-hardening response allows WTaTiVZr to sustain more plastic deformation than pure tungsten.
The proposed deformation response delays crack nucleation and propagation relative to pure tungsten.
Delayed crack nucleation and propagation increase the toughness of WTaTiVZr.
The hypothesized advantage is expected to be significant during sustained high-temperature loading typical of plasma-facing components.
The effect may differ at lower temperatures or in substantially different environments.
Using identical processing histories will ensure comparable starting microstructures in WTaTiVZr and commercially pure tungsten.
A controlled comparison should subject WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten to identical sustained-creep or cyclic-loading conditions at high temperature.
Plastic strain, toughness, dislocation density, and heterogeneous deformation can be measured to test the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a statistically significant improvement in plastic strain or toughness relative to pure tungsten would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the predicted lattice-distortion-attributable change in dislocation behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
